title: the Yaksha's questions
hook: Yudhishthira reaches the lake, reads the scene, and agrees to answer; the questions begin

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Yaksha's questions went unanswered four times: thirst, grief, aim and strength, and four brothers on the shore. Your line was the lake wants to be answered. Did you ask what something wanted before pushing? Day eight hundred three.
screen: `THE YAKSHA'S QUESTIONS.` · `FOUR BROTHERS ON THE SHORE.`

segments.voice: The last brother comes alone. Yudhishthira has waited under the tree as long as he can, and now he follows the cranes himself. He finds the lake, and all four of his brothers lying beside it. He weeps over each of them by name, and remembers what each one was to him. And then, through his grief, he does something none of them did. He looks. Before he touches the water, he reads the shore.
screen: `THE LAST BROTHER COMES ALONE.` → `HE WEEPS OVER EACH ONE.` → `THEN HE LOOKS.`

segments.voice: What Yudhishthira sees doesn't add up. There are no wounds on his brothers. There are no footprints of an enemy. Their faces haven't changed color, so he doesn't think it's poison. Whatever did this, he reasons, is something greater than an ordinary foe. He steps down into the water, and the voice comes. I am a crane, it says. I killed your brothers. Answer my questions, or you'll be the fifth. Yudhishthira doesn't believe it. No bird could do this, he says. Who are you? And then he sees it: a yaksha, a huge spirit, towering over the lake, speaking from up in a tree. Yudhishthira doesn't shoot, or fight, or drink. He says something quiet instead. I don't want what's yours. Ask, and I'll answer as well as I'm able. And so the questions begin. Some of them sound like riddles. What is heavier than the earth? Yudhishthira answers: a mother. What is higher than the sky? A father. What is faster than the wind? The mind. What is more numerous than blades of grass? Our thoughts. Look at what those four answers do. The yaksha asks about the size of the world, and Yudhishthira answers with a family, and a mind. Weight becomes a mother's claim on us. Height becomes a father's. Speed and number turn inward, to what happens behind the eyes. The questions point outward, and the answers come home. Watch for that in the answers still to come.
screen: `NO WOUNDS, NO FOOTPRINTS.` · `I AM A CRANE. WHO ARE YOU?` · `I'LL ANSWER AS WELL AS I'M ABLE.` · then, large: `HEAVIER THAN THE EARTH? A MOTHER.`

segments.voice: Settle, and let the breath slow down. Now watch your thoughts arrive, the way you'd watch blades of grass in a field: one, then another, then too many to follow. Don't count them. Don't pick any up. Just notice how many there are, and how fast the mind runs after them, faster than the wind, as Yudhishthira says. Breathe in, and see a thought. Breathe out, and let it go back into the field. If you pray, you can let the thoughts pass through your prayer. The bell holds the time.
Yaksha-prashna, the yaksha's questions, which Yudhishthira is the first to answer. The brother who stops to look, offers to answer, and turns every question about the world back home. Today's word.
Your line: weight becomes a mother's claim. Today, before you react to something that looks wrong, look closely once more. Day eight hundred three.

howItsDone: In the epic, the yaksha's questions often sound like riddles, and Yudhishthira's answers keep pointing back to family, mind and conduct.

match.prompt: the first answers — tap the pairs.

myth: Yudhishthira found wounds on his brothers
there were no wounds and no footprints, which is why he suspected something more than an enemy.
the voice first claimed to be a crane
Yudhishthira said no bird could do this, and asked who it really was.
he said he did not want what was the yaksha's, and offered to answer.

fork.setup: you're Yudhishthira. four brothers lie dead by the lake, you're dying of thirst, and a voice says answer first. what do you do?
options: drink quickly, before the voice can stop you.
ask who it is, and agree to answer.
fork.reveal: he asks who it is, sees a yaksha, and says: I don't want what's yours. ask, and I'll answer as well as I'm able.

original.note: Sanskrit: yaksha-prashna, the yaksha's questions; prashna means a question.

trapdoor: what you thought: a quiz that Yudhishthira happens to be good at.
what it means: he stops, reads the scene, refuses to take what isn't his, and only then answers.
what a scholar hears: the answers turn the world's measures, weight, height, speed, number, back to family and the mind.

sources.ref: Mahabharata, Vana Parva (Aranyaka Parva), the episode of the Yaksha's questions: Yudhishthira at the lake; the crane and the yaksha; the first questions (heavier than the earth, higher than the sky, faster than the wind, more numerous than grass)

notes: All paraphrase. Confirm in Ganguli: Yudhishthira notes no wounds, no footprints, unchanged faces (ruling out poison); the voice first claims to be a crane; the yaksha's appearance beside a tree; Yudhishthira's reply that he does not covet what is the yaksha's.

Confirm the four answers: mother weightier than the earth, father higher than heaven, mind fleeter than wind, thoughts more numerous than grass. Other questions come earlier in the sequence in Ganguli; the script presents these as 'some of them'.
Original यक्षप्रश्न: confirm as the traditional name of the episode.

Editor pass: these four are not the first questions in Ganguli, so the hook no longer calls them 'the first'; 'this is how the whole contest will go' softened; the practice no longer gives the 'faster than the wind' answer to thoughts (the text gives it to the mind); garbled prayer line fixed; howItsDone no longer claims how the episode is 'often taught'.
Audit: Ganguli places the yaksha 'staying on a tree', not beside one; 'speaking from beside a tree' became 'from up in a tree'. Cut the leftover templated 'Today, ...' hook closer.
